title: TutorLLM: Customizing Learning Recommendations with Knowledge Tracing and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
venue: Proceedings of the 18th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2024)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a key limitation of large language models in education: although tools such as ChatGPT can answer a wide range of student questions, they often lack personalization and may provide irrelevant or inaccurate responses. The authors aim to improve educational usefulness by combining the flexibility of LLMs with student modeling and course-specific retrieval, asking whether a personalized recommender LLM can improve student experience and learning outcomes compared with a general-purpose LLM alone.

The proposed intervention, TutorLLM, integrates three components: a knowledge tracing module based on the MLFBK model to estimate students’ learning states, a scraper that collects course-specific textual content from online learning pages, and a retrieval-augmented GPT-4-based LLM that uses both the student model and retrieved course materials to generate personalized responses and study recommendations. The system was implemented as a Chrome browser plugin that students could use during online study sessions and after class for tailored recommendations of additional materials.

The empirical evaluation was conducted as a two-week field study with 30 first-year undergraduate students enrolled in a linear algebra module at the University of Southampton. Students were randomly allocated to three groups: a general-LLM control group, a hybrid group that used general LLM first and TutorLLM second, and a TutorLLM group that used TutorLLM throughout. The study took place in an online course context, with daily quizzes and a final test used to assess performance, alongside usability and user experience questionnaires for students using TutorLLM.

The main conclusions are that TutorLLM showed promise for improving the learning experience, with higher user satisfaction, strong usability scores, greater engagement time, and modest gains in quiz performance relative to general LLM use. However, the differences in academic performance were not statistically significant in this small study. The authors conclude that the approach is promising but requires further validation with larger samples, longer durations, and broader disciplinary settings.

identified_tools.name: TutorLLM
identified_tools.description: A personalized educational recommender LLM system that combines knowledge tracing (MLFBK), retrieval-augmented generation, a web-content scraper, and GPT-4 to provide course-specific answers and personalized study recommendations.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a Chrome browser plugin for undergraduate linear algebra learning, where students asked questions during online study sessions and received personalized post-session study material recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: In a two-week field study with 30 first-year undergraduate students in a linear algebra module, the TutorLLM group had the highest overall mean score (74.48) versus the hybrid LLM group (72.81) and general LLM group (71.97). However, ANOVA on final exam scores found no statistically significant difference across groups (F=0.795, p=0.462), although the authors note a trend toward improved performance and describe this as about a 5% improvement in quiz scores compared to general LLMs.
findings.measure: Daily quizzes and final comprehensive linear algebra exam scores

findings.finding_summary: TutorLLM received generally positive usability ratings, with an average System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 76.35 and median 79. Score variability was moderate (SD=14.46), the Shapiro-Wilk test supported normality (p=0.721), and bootstrap analysis estimated the median's 95% confidence interval as 68.5 to 83.

User experience ratings for TutorLLM were positive, with average scores of 3.50 for Comfort Level, 3.40 for Continue Willingness, and 3.61 for User Satisfaction on 5-point scales. The paper also reports a 10% increase in user satisfaction compared to the general LLM approach and moderate positive correlations among CL, CW, and US (0.53, 0.45, and 0.40 respectively).
findings.measure: User Experience questionnaire: Comfort Level, Continue Willingness, and User Satisfaction

findings.finding_summary: Students using TutorLLM spent 36% more time engaging with the system than students using general LLMs. The authors interpret this as indicating higher satisfaction and willingness to invest time in the personalized system.
findings.measure: Duration of LLM usage / engagement time

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model family used as a general-purpose conversational AI assistant.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the control condition via the general web version of ChatGPT-4 for students to ask questions during online linear algebra study, without personalized recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: The control group using the general web version of ChatGPT-4 had an overall mean score of 71.97, compared with 74.48 for TutorLLM and 72.81 for the hybrid LLM group. ANOVA on final exam scores showed no statistically significant variance across groups (F=0.795, p=0.462).
findings.measure: Daily quizzes and final comprehensive linear algebra exam scores

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical controlled field study with random allocation and a crossover element, but the sample is small (n=30) and the main academic outcome was not statistically significant. The design is stronger than descriptive work, yet falls short of high-certainty evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported impacts are promising but mostly unclear in magnitude, with no effect sizes reported and no statistically significant academic improvement on final exam analysis. Positive usability, satisfaction, and engagement findings support some practical benefit, but overall impact remains modest/uncertain.
